<reason>Both sides accepted the underlying duty and fought the mechanism question cleanly, but B did more analytical work. When A pivoted mid-debate to "fine the platform, scaled to revenue," B exploited the shift twice: (1) showing it silently reintroduces the bureaucratic apparatus A had earlier mocked in CON's scorecard proposal, and (2) showing the structural incentive it creates—platforms dropping risky small clients to avoid liability—which A never neutralized beyond asserting "that's not a reason to keep the lock free." B's constructive alternative (authorization-conditioned remediation orders tied directly to the broken pathway, rather than a revenue-based bill that can be paid while exiting the customer) was more original and was defended with a sharper closing distinction between "a bill regardless of fix" and "a remedy with fix built in." A's rebuttals were rhetorically tight ("price the lock," "cheapest path") but repeated the same framing across rounds rather than directly dismantling B's exit-incentive and audit-chilling mechanisms, leaving those live at the close.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1/2 sequence (B2.2-B2.3, extended in B4.2-B4.3) turning A's "fine the platform, scale to revenue" pivot into both a bureaucracy concession and a customer-dropping incentive was the most damaging unanswered pressure point in the debate.</best_rebuttal>
